title: Prenatal Serum Screening: Maternal AFP, Neural Tube Defects and the Down Syndrome Screen
summary: Learn why open neural tube defects raise maternal serum AFP, how MoM results and cutoffs are read, why most elevations are not neural tube defects, how the triple, quad and combined screens perform for Down syndrome, and where folic acid fits in prevention.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 26 Hit 6 (Down syndrome screening performance), Hit 7 (maternal serum AFP), Hit 12 (folic acid and the MRC trial) and Trap 4 (elevated MSAFP is not a diagnosis; MoM adjustment). Checked against the ACMG 2009 guideline (Driscoll and Gross), Kim 2023, Salih 2014, Głowska-Ciemny 2024 and Czeizel 2013. Qualified: Hit 6 quad 94–96% and integrated ~98% at <0.5% (ACMG: quad ~75% under 35 and >80% at 35 or older, integrated 93–96%, at about 5% screen positive; rv-down-screen-detection); Hit 6 “advanced maternal age = 35” lacks context (ACMG: no longer the cutoff for offering invasive testing; rv-down-ama-35); Hit 7 “peaks at 12–14 weeks, falls ~10%/week” (the late-first-trimester peak is fetal serum; sources disagree on the maternal curve; rv-msafp-peak-timing); MSAFP as the NTD screen (ultrasound now recommended instead of MSAFP in some national guidelines, ACOG and JOGC/SOGC as summarised by Kim 2023; rv-msafp-vs-ultrasound). Not taught: Trap 4’s numerical race (~10–15%) and diabetes (~20%) adjustments, the first-trimester serum-only 82–87% figure, and the exact MRC 72% value (Czeizel 2013 reports 71%). ACOG Practice Bulletins 187 and the SOGC guideline 410 were not open access and were not read.

objectives: Explain why open, but not closed, neural tube defects raise maternal serum AFP.
Interpret an MSAFP result in MoM, including singleton and twin cutoffs and the effect of wrong dates.
List non-NTD causes of an elevated MSAFP and the follow-up steps.
Recognise the second-trimester marker patterns of trisomy 21 and trisomy 18 and the approximate detection rates of the main screens.
State the evidence for periconceptional folic acid in NTD prevention.

scenes.title: Three second-trimester screens
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three maternal serum screening reports. (1) Singleton pregnancy, sample at 17 weeks by ultrasound dates: AFP 3.1 MoM. (2) A twin pregnancy at 17 weeks: AFP 3.1 MoM. (3) Quad screen at 16 weeks: AFP low, unconjugated estriol low, hCG high, inhibin A high. Question token: “Neural tube defect, twins, or Down syndrome risk?”

cues.text: Three second-trimester screening reports arrive. A singleton pregnancy at seventeen weeks has a maternal serum AFP of 3.1 multiples of the median.
A twin pregnancy has the same AFP value. And a quad screen shows low AFP and estriol, with high hCG and inhibin A.
Which one points to a neural tube defect, which is explained by twins, and which raises the risk of Down syndrome?

props.label: NTD, twins, or Down syndrome risk?

scenes.title: Where maternal AFP comes from
scenes.altText: Schematic: fetus, amniotic fluid and maternal blood as three boxes linked by arrows. AFP is a fetal glycoprotein made first by the yolk sac and then mainly by the fetal liver; fetal serum levels peak near the end of the first trimester. AFP passes into amniotic fluid and then into maternal blood, where the concentration is far lower (maternal serum is roughly 1/100 of amniotic fluid). An open neural tube defect exposes fetal tissue, so more AFP leaks into amniotic fluid and maternal serum; a skin-covered (closed) defect does not. Results are reported as multiples of the median (MoM), adjusted for gestational age, maternal weight, race, insulin-dependent diabetes, number of fetuses and family history. Prevention card: periconceptional folic acid.

cues.text: AFP is a fetal protein, made first by the yolk sac and then mainly by the fetal liver. Fetal blood levels peak near the end of the first trimester.

It passes into the amniotic fluid and then, in much smaller amounts, into the mother’s blood. An open neural tube defect exposes fetal tissue, so extra AFP leaks out. A skin-covered defect does not leak.
Because AFP changes with gestational age, results are given as multiples of the median, adjusted for maternal weight, race, insulin-dependent diabetes, the number of fetuses and family history.

Prevention comes before screening. In the Medical Research Council trial, four milligrams of folic acid cut recurrence by about seventy percent, and in 1992 the CDC advised 0.4 milligrams daily for every woman who could become pregnant.

props.label: Open defect leaks AFP · closed (skin-covered) defect does not

scenes.title: An elevated MSAFP is a screen, not a diagnosis
scenes.altText: Cutoff card: screening window 15–20 weeks (best 16–18); screen positive at about 2.0–2.5 MoM in singletons and 4.0–5.0 MoM in twins, set by each laboratory. Detection card: anencephaly about 95% or more; open spina bifida about 65–80%; closed defects (about 20% of spinal NTDs) are not detected. Causes card: when MSAFP is elevated, only about 2–4% of pregnancies have an NTD; other causes are underestimated gestational age, multiple gestation, abdominal wall defects (gastroschisis, omphalocele), fetal death and placental problems, and unexplained elevations carry a higher risk of adverse outcomes. Follow-up card: confirm dates (reinterpret if they change by more than 10 days), then targeted ultrasound and/or amniocentesis for amniotic fluid AFP and acetylcholinesterase.

cues.text: Maternal serum AFP is drawn between fifteen and twenty weeks, ideally sixteen to eighteen. A screen is positive at about 2.0 to 2.5 multiples of the median in a singleton, and 4.0 to 5.0 in twins. Each lab sets its own cutoff.

At those cutoffs it detects about ninety-five percent of anencephaly but only sixty-five to eighty percent of open spina bifida. Closed, skin-covered defects are missed; one review puts them at about one in five spinal defects.
Most elevations are not neural tube defects: only about two to four percent are. Wrong dates, twins, abdominal wall defects, fetal death and placental problems also raise AFP.

So the next steps are to confirm the dates, because a change of more than ten days means the result must be reinterpreted, and then a targeted ultrasound, with amniotic fluid AFP and acetylcholinesterase if needed.

scenes.title: Reading the Down syndrome screen
scenes.altText: Marker table: in Down syndrome (trisomy 21), second-trimester AFP and unconjugated estriol (uE3) are usually low while hCG and dimeric inhibin A are high; in trisomy 18, AFP, hCG and uE3 are all low. First trimester: PAPP-A low and hCG high in trisomy 21, with nuchal translucency. Detection bar (as summarised by ACMG 2009; screen-positive rate stated as 5% for the quad screen under 35 and for first-trimester combined): triple screen ~65%; quad screen ~75% under age 35 and >80% at 35 or older; first-trimester combined (nuchal translucency + PAPP-A + hCG) 79–90%; serum integrated ~88%; integrated 93–96% (combined figures from modelling). Hook answers: (1) singleton 3.1 MoM: screen positive for open NTD → confirm dates, targeted ultrasound; (2) twins 3.1 MoM: below the twin cutoff of 4.0–5.0 MoM; (3) quad pattern: increased Down syndrome risk → counselling and the option of diagnostic testing.

cues.text: In Down syndrome, the second-trimester pattern is low AFP and low estriol, with high hCG and high inhibin A. In trisomy 18, AFP, hCG and estriol are all low.

Adding markers raises detection. In the ACMG summary, the triple screen finds about sixty-five percent of Down syndrome, the quad screen about seventy-five to over eighty, first-trimester combined screening seventy-nine to ninety, and integrated screening ninety-three to ninety-six.
Back to the hook. The singleton at 3.1 multiples of the median is screen positive: confirm the dates and do a targeted ultrasound. The same value in twins is below the twin cutoff.
The quad pattern raises the risk of Down syndrome. That calls for counselling and an offer of diagnostic testing, not a diagnosis.

props.title: Hook answers
lines: 3 Higher DS risk → counsel, offer testing

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “Elevated MSAFP means a neural tube defect” (✓ only about 2–4% are; check dates and twins, then targeted ultrasound); “A normal MSAFP rules out an NTD” (✓ closed defects do not leak, and a share of open defects is missed); “The quad screen detects about 95% of Down syndrome, and only women 35 or older need it” (✓ about 75% under 35 and over 80% at 35 or older; screening and diagnostic testing are offered regardless of age).

cues.text: Trap one: an elevated AFP means a neural tube defect. No: only a small fraction are. Check dates and twins first, then image.
Trap two: a normal AFP rules out a neural tube defect. No: closed defects do not leak, and some open ones are missed.

Trap three: the quad screen finds about ninety-five percent of Down syndrome, and only women over thirty-five need it. No: it finds about three quarters in younger women, a little over eighty percent in older women, and screening is offered to women of any age.

props.title: ✗ “High MSAFP = neural tube defect.”
lines: ✓ Only ~2–4% are; dates, twins, then ultrasound

props.title: ✗ “Normal MSAFP rules out an NTD.”
lines: ✓ Closed defects don’t leak; some open ones missed

scenes.title: Leaky roof, HI and low
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “AFP is a leak detector: an open roof (open defect) leaks AFP, a closed roof does not. For Down syndrome, the HI markers are high (hCG, Inhibin A) and the other two are low (AFP, Estriol).” Tokens: open roof leaks · closed roof dry · hCG + inhibin A high · AFP + estriol low. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: AFP is a leak detector. An open roof leaks, a closed roof stays dry. For Down syndrome, think “HI”: hCG and inhibin A are high, while AFP and estriol are low.

Where it breaks: other leaks raise AFP too, such as twins, wrong dates and abdominal wall defects; the detection figures for combined screens come from modelling; and in some national guidelines ultrasound now leads neural tube defect screening.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Elevated MSAFP = screen positive: confirm dates and twins, then targeted ultrasound · closed defects are missed”, “Down syndrome: AFP and estriol low, hCG and inhibin A high · quad ~75% to >80%”.

cues.text: An elevated maternal serum AFP is a screen that sends you to confirm dates and fetal number and then to targeted ultrasound, it misses closed defects, and in Down syndrome AFP and estriol fall while hCG and inhibin A rise.

props.label: High MSAFP → dates, twins, ultrasound · closed defects missed
Down syndrome: AFP + uE3 ↓ · hCG + inhibin A ↑ · quad ~75% to >80%

explanation.what: Plain language: the fetus makes a protein called AFP, and a little of it reaches the mother’s blood. If the spine or skull is open, extra AFP leaks out, so a high level flags the pregnancy for a closer look. But many other things also raise AFP, so it is a screening test, not a diagnosis. The same blood sample, with a few more markers, estimates the chance of Down syndrome. Scientific terms: alpha-fetoprotein (AFP), maternal serum AFP (MSAFP), multiples of the median (MoM), open neural tube defect (ONTD), anencephaly, open spina bifida, closed spinal dysraphism, amniotic fluid AFP, acetylcholinesterase, triple and quad screen, unconjugated estriol (uE3), dimeric inhibin A, PAPP-A, nuchal translucency, integrated and sequential screening, periconceptional folic acid.
explanation.why: AFP is a fetal protein that crosses into amniotic fluid and maternal blood; exposed fetal tissue in an open defect increases that transfer. Because AFP changes with gestational age and with maternal and pregnancy factors, results are normalised as MoM and adjusted. In trisomy 21, AFP and estriol are typically lower and hCG and inhibin A higher, and the screen combines these with maternal age into a risk estimate.
explanation.measure: MSAFP: 15–20 weeks (best 16–18). Screen positive about 2.0–2.5 MoM (singleton) or 4.0–5.0 MoM (twins); laboratory-specific. Detection: anencephaly about 95% or more; open spina bifida 65–80%; closed defects not detected. Only about 2–4% of elevations are NTDs. Reinterpret if dates change by more than 10 days; redraw if the sample was taken before 15 weeks. Follow-up: targeted ultrasound and/or amniotic fluid AFP with acetylcholinesterase. Down syndrome detection at about 5% screen positive: triple ~65%; quad ~75% (<35 y) and >80% (≥35 y); first-trimester combined 79–90%; serum integrated ~88%; integrated 93–96% (modelled). Folic acid: MRC trial (4 mg) reduced recurrence about 71%; CDC 1992: 0.4 mg/day for women who could become pregnant.
explanation.differs: Open vs closed NTD (leaks AFP vs does not); trisomy 21 (AFP and uE3 low, hCG and inhibin A high) vs trisomy 18 (AFP, hCG and uE3 all low); singleton vs twin cutoffs; screen positive vs diagnosis.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: the next step after an elevated MSAFP; which defect MSAFP misses; the quad-screen pattern of Down syndrome; why a twin pregnancy or wrong dates changes interpretation; or the trial that proved folic acid prevents NTD recurrence.

questions.stem: A singleton pregnancy at 17 weeks has a maternal serum AFP of 3.1 MoM. What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Confirm gestational age and fetal number, then targeted ultrasound
options.rationale: Correct. An elevated MSAFP is a screen; wrong dates and twins must be excluded and the fetus imaged, with amniotic fluid AFP and acetylcholinesterase if needed.

options.text: Report a diagnosis of open spina bifida
options.rationale: Incorrect. Only a small fraction (about 2–4%) of elevated results are neural tube defects.
Incorrect. The result is screen positive and needs follow-up.

options.text: Repeat MSAFP in the third trimester
options.rationale: Incorrect. The screening window is 15–20 weeks; follow-up is imaging, not a late repeat.

questions.stem: Which second-trimester quad-screen pattern is typical of a pregnancy with Down syndrome (trisomy 21)?

options.text: AFP low, uE3 low, hCG high, inhibin A high
options.rationale: Correct. AFP and unconjugated estriol are lower, hCG and dimeric inhibin A higher.

options.text: AFP low, uE3 low, hCG low, inhibin A normal
options.rationale: Incorrect. Low AFP, uE3 and hCG together suggest trisomy 18.

options.text: AFP high, uE3 normal, hCG normal, inhibin A normal
options.rationale: Incorrect. An isolated high AFP points to an open NTD or another leak, not trisomy 21.

options.text: AFP high, uE3 high, hCG low, inhibin A low
options.rationale: Incorrect. Every marker moves in the opposite direction to trisomy 21.

questions.stem: Which fetal condition is maternal serum AFP screening least likely to detect?

options.rationale: Correct. Closed defects do not expose fetal tissue, so AFP does not leak.
Incorrect. MSAFP detects about 95% or more of anencephaly.
Incorrect. MSAFP detects about 65–80% of open spina bifida.
Incorrect. Abdominal wall defects are a recognised cause of elevated MSAFP.

AFP from yolk sac then fetal liver; fetal serum peak around 9–13 weeks; maternal serum about 1/100 of amniotic fluid and rising until about 32 weeks; 2.5 MoM criterion; detection ~95% anencephaly and 65–80% open spinal NTDs; closed type ~20% of spinal NTDs and not detected by MSAFP; ~25% false negatives; only 2–4% of elevations are NTDs; causes of abnormal MSAFP (Table 1); unexplained elevation and adverse outcomes; its report that some countries (citing ACOG Practice Bulletin 187 and the Canadian JOGC/SOGC guideline) now recommend mid-trimester ultrasound instead of MSAFP, the JOGC naming it the primary NTD screen with MSAFP of limited use, and one comparison of 96% vs 75% detection.

references.usedFor: Full text. AFP leaks into amniotic fluid and maternal blood with open defects; at a 2.5 MoM cutoff anencephaly detection >95% and open NTDs 65–70%; closed NTDs (about 10% of lesions in this review) do not raise AFP; other causes include fetal demise, omphalocele and gastroschisis; amniotic AFP with acetylcholinesterase after ultrasound; periconceptional folic acid lowers NTD prevalence.

Its description of the maternal curve (decreasing after week 6) differs from Kim 2023, so the lesson does not teach a maternal peak week.

claims.text: AFP made by yolk sac then fetal liver; fetal serum peak late first trimester; passes into amniotic fluid and maternal blood; open defects leak, closed defects do not.
MoM reporting and adjustment factors; >10-day dating change requires reinterpretation; sample before 15 weeks redrawn.
Window 15–20 weeks; cutoffs 2.0–2.5 MoM singleton and 4.0–5.0 MoM twins; detection ≥95% anencephaly, 65–80% open spina bifida; closed defects missed (~20% of spinal NTDs).
claims.note: Open-NTD detection ranges differ between sources (Kim 2023 65–80%, Salih 2014 65–70%, ACMG 2009 75–90% for ONTDs); the closed-defect share is ~20% of spinal NTDs in Kim 2023 and ~10% of lesions in Salih 2014.

claims.text: Only about 2–4% of elevations are NTDs; other causes (dates, twins, abdominal wall defects, fetal death, placental problems); follow-up by targeted ultrasound and amniotic AFP with acetylcholinesterase.
Ultrasound now leads NTD screening in some national guidelines.
claims.note: ACOG Practice Bulletin 187 and SOGC guideline 410 were not read directly; their content is as summarised by Kim 2023.

claims.text: Trisomy 21 and 18 marker directions; detection of triple, quad, first-trimester combined, serum integrated and integrated screening at about 5% screen positive; screening offered regardless of maternal age.
MRC trial: 4 mg folic acid reduced NTD recurrence by about 71%; CDC 1992: 0.4 mg/day.

Reviewer figures not taught: Black women ~10–15% higher and insulin-dependent diabetes ~20% lower MSAFP; MSAFP peak at 12–14 weeks falling ~10%/week; first-trimester PAPP-A + β-hCG 82–87%; integrated ~98% at <0.5% false positive.
claims.note: No open source read for this lesson gives the race or diabetes magnitudes; sources disagree on the maternal AFP curve; the detection figures differ from ACMG 2009.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 26 Hit 6 gives quad-screen detection of 94–96% and integrated ~98% at <0.5% false positive. ACMG 2009 (Driscoll and Gross) gives the quad screen ~75% under 35 and >80% at 35 or older, and integrated screening 93–96%, with combined-screen figures based on modelling; it gives no figure near 98% at <0.5% false positive (register flag rv-down-screen-detection).

Ch. 26 Hit 6 states “advanced maternal age = 35 years” without context. ACMG 2009 says age 35 at delivery was the historical trigger for offering diagnostic testing, but maternal age 35 is no longer recommended as the cutoff for offering invasive diagnostic testing and age alone is a poor screening criterion; all women are offered screening and the option of diagnostic testing regardless of age (register flag rv-down-ama-35).

Ch. 26 Hit 7 says AFP “peaks at 12–14 weeks, falls ~10%/week in the second trimester”. Kim 2023 places the peak around 9–13 weeks in fetal serum and says maternal serum AFP keeps rising until about 32 weeks; Głowska-Ciemny 2024 describes the maternal curve differently. The lesson teaches only that AFP must be read against the exact gestational week (register flag rv-msafp-peak-timing).

Ch. 26 Hit 7 and Trap 4 present MSAFP as the NTD screen. Kim 2023 reports that some countries (citing ACOG Practice Bulletin 187 and the Canadian JOGC/SOGC guideline) now recommend mid-trimester ultrasound instead of MSAFP, the JOGC naming it the primary NTD screen with MSAFP of limited use; practice is guideline- and country-dependent, and Philippine practice is not covered (register flag rv-msafp-vs-ultrasound).

morphology.note: No ultrasound or clinical images; compartments and marker patterns shown as cards.

verification.notes: 7 factual claims checked against ACMG 2009 (Driscoll and Gross), Kim 2023, Salih 2014, Głowska-Ciemny 2024 and Czeizel 2013 (all full texts read via Europe PMC); 1 pending (reviewer race and diabetes adjustment magnitudes, AFP peak timing and some detection figures, not taught). ACOG and SOGC guidelines were not open access and were not read. No human expert has reviewed this lesson.
